cls: Amino-acid analogue / GABA-A modulator and anti-amyloid agent (tramiprosate; marketed as a nutraceutical for cognitive/neuronal support)
pharm: A small aminosulfonate analogue of taurine and GABA that binds soluble beta-amyloid peptide to inhibit amyloid aggregation/fibril formation and also acts as a partial GABA-A receptor agonist, proposed to support neuronal function.
quick: Commonly 100 mg orally once daily as a supplement (investigational trials used ~100-150 mg twice daily)
May be taken with or without food
Avoid excess; both act on GABAergic systems
Tolerability (GI, mood); no established laboratory monitoring
summary: Homotaurine (3-amino-1-propanesulfonic acid; the drug-development name is tramiprosate) is a small naturally occurring aminosulfonic acid, structurally related to taurine and GABA. It was investigated as a disease-modifying anti-amyloid agent for Alzheimer disease - binding soluble beta-amyloid and inhibiting its aggregation into neurotoxic fibrils - but the pivotal phase 3 trials did not meet their primary endpoints, so it is NOT an approved drug for Alzheimer disease and is NOT FDA-approved. It is marketed in several countries (notably in Europe and Canada) as a NUTRACEUTICAL/dietary supplement for memory and neuronal support, typically at 100 mg once daily; investigational trials used higher doses (around 100-150 mg twice daily). It is generally well tolerated, with mild gastrointestinal effects and occasional nausea, mood or sleep changes reported; robust clinical efficacy and long-term safety data are limited. Because it is a supplement rather than an approved medicine, no formal FDA prescribing information exists; information here is drawn from manufacturer/supplement information and the clinical trial literature.
indications: Marketed (as a nutraceutical/dietary supplement) to support memory and cognitive/neuronal function - NOT an approved treatment for any disease
Investigated (as tramiprosate) for slowing progression of mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease - efficacy not established in pivotal trials

dosage.n: Marketed as a supplement; follow the specific product directions
Trial dosing - efficacy not established; not an approved regimen

admin: Take the oral dose with or without food, consistently each day
Recognise that it is sold as a dietary supplement, not an approved medicine, so quality/standardisation varies by product
Do not use as a substitute for evidence-based treatment of dementia or any diagnosed condition
Counsel patients to inform their physician, especially if taking other CNS-active drugs
Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding given lack of safety data
Discontinue if poorly tolerated (gastrointestinal upset, mood or sleep disturbance)
moa: Homotaurine (tramiprosate) is a small aminosulfonate that mimics the glycosaminoglycan binding region of beta-amyloid. It binds preferentially to soluble beta-amyloid (Abeta) peptide, interfering with its self-aggregation and the formation of neurotoxic oligomers and fibrils, the proposed disease-modifying mechanism in Alzheimer disease. As a structural analogue of GABA and taurine it also acts as a partial agonist at GABA-A receptors, which may contribute to neuromodulatory and neuroprotective effects. Despite this rationale, clinical trials did not demonstrate a clear cognitive benefit.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to homotaurine or product components
relative: Concurrent use of other GABAergic/CNS depressants
Significant renal or hepatic impairment (limited data)
monitor: Mood, sleep and any neuropsychiatric changes
Cognitive status if used for cognitive complaints (no validated surrogate)

preg: There are insufficient data on the use of homotaurine in pregnancy; as a non-essential supplement it should be avoided during pregnancy.
lact: There are insufficient data on homotaurine during breastfeeding; it should be avoided while nursing.
renal: Homotaurine is a small, water-soluble molecule largely excreted by the kidneys; there are limited specific data in renal impairment, so use with caution and consider lower exposure if renal function is reduced.
hepatic: There are limited specific data in hepatic impairment; use with caution.

moderate: GABAergic and CNS-depressant drugs (benzodiazepines, alcohol, sedatives) - potential additive central effects given partial GABA-A agonism
minor: No well-characterised pharmacokinetic drug interactions are established
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; no major food interaction described.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol because both act on GABAergic neurotransmission.

serious: Generally none well established at supplement doses; data limited
emergency: Severe allergic reaction (rare; seek care for rash, swelling, breathing difficulty)

monitoring: Mood, sleep and any neuropsychiatric symptoms
Overall benefit if used for cognitive complaints (no validated monitoring marker)
counsel: This is a dietary supplement, not an approved medicine - it has not been proven to treat or prevent Alzheimer disease or dementia
Take it consistently as directed and tell your doctor you are using it, especially if you take other brain/nerve medicines
Mild stomach upset, nausea or headache can occur; stop and ask your doctor if these are troublesome
Do not use it instead of recommended treatment for a diagnosed condition
Avoid it if you are pregnant or breastfeeding
pk: Not well characterised for clinical effect
Oral Tmax within a few hours
Short - on the order of a few hours (limited data)
Store at room temperature, protected from moisture, per product label
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - homotaurine (tramiprosate) is sold as a nutraceutical/dietary supplement (mainly in Europe/Canada); information here comes from supplement/EMA-type product information and clinical-trial literature
Developed as an anti-amyloid agent for Alzheimer disease but pivotal phase 3 trials did NOT meet their primary endpoints - efficacy is not established
Structural analogue of taurine/GABA - binds soluble beta-amyloid and is a partial GABA-A agonist
Typical supplement dose is 100 mg once daily; trials used ~100-150 mg twice daily
Generally well tolerated (mild GI effects); avoid in pregnancy/breastfeeding and be cautious with other CNS depressants
Should not replace evidence-based dementia care
missed: If a dose is missed, take it when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it. Do not double up. As a supplement, an occasional missed dose is not harmful.
overdose: There is little information on overdose. Excessive intake would be expected to cause gastrointestinal upset and possibly sedation or mood effects from GABAergic activity. Management is supportive; discontinue the supplement and seek medical advice for significant symptoms.
